claims.text: The baseline alloy is eutectic Al0.7CoCrFeNi produced by conventional casting.
Conventionally cast eutectic Al0.7CoCrFeNi has a standard lamellar microstructure.
The proposed intervention is addition of approximately 5–7 at% Zr during casting followed by rapid annealing.
Rapid annealing at approximately 850°C for tens of seconds will promote homogeneous Zr distribution while suppressing coarse segregation.
The combined Zr addition and rapid annealing treatment will produce a modified lamellar microstructure.
The intervention will refine the interlamellar spacing.
Zr incorporation will induce local lattice distortions in the alloy.
Zr has a larger atomic size than the base-alloy elements.
Zr-induced local lattice distortions will enhance solid-solution strengthening.
Refined interlamellar spacing will improve strain partitioning between the constituent phases.
Improved strain partitioning will increase work hardening.
Increased work hardening will delay necking and thereby improve ductility.
The Zr-modified and rapidly annealed alloy will have higher yield strength than the conventional Zr-free alloy.
The Zr-modified and rapidly annealed alloy will have greater ductility than the conventional Zr-free alloy.
The simultaneous strength and ductility improvement requires uniform Zr distribution without coarse segregation.
Excessive Zr content or prolonged heat treatment may cause phase separation or coarse microstructures.
Phase separation or coarse microstructure formation may negate the proposed mechanical benefits.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in both yield strength and ductility relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The stated baseline is an as-cast, conventionally processed Zr-free alloy, whereas the experimental control is Zr-free but receives the same rapid heat treatment as the modified alloy. These are different comparators, so the predicted outcome and falsification test do not use a single consistent baseline.

The boundary excludes conditions that produce substantial Zr segregation or coarse phases, but the falsification rule treats observation of such features as falsifying the hypothesis. A result outside the hypothesis's stated processing window does not by itself test the conditional claim.
